title: Bengaluru Engineer Builds AI App That Turns Potholes Into Accountable Complaints
excerpt: Gaurav Sen's open-source Pothole Reporter matches dashcam-detected road damage to government contracts and drafts a ready-to-send complaint — photo, location, and tender reference — in about four seconds.
body:
• Bengaluru engineer Gaurav Sen has built Pothole Reporter, an open-source Android app that turns a dashcam drive into a ready-to-send road complaint — photo, coordinates, and tender reference — in about four seconds.
  • The system pairs a camera, GPS, and accelerometer with OpenAI's vision models to detect potholes of different sizes, then scans thousands of government road tenders to match each defect to the right road contract.
  • A deliberate guardrail: it names a contractor only when official records confirm the exact road segment, work scope, award, owner, and warranty — otherwise it still drafts a documented complaint to the right office.
  • The app is free and open-source under an MIT license (built with Deepanshu Pathak); commuters in India can download it, supply their own OpenAI API key, and file evidence-backed complaints instead of unheeded one-line reports.

Bengaluru engineer Gaurav Sen has built an AI-powered app that does what every frustrated commuter wishes they could do: spot a pothole, identify who is responsible for that stretch of road, and draft a ready-to-send complaint — all in about four seconds. The system, called Pothole Reporter, went viral after Sen demonstrated it on Instagram in collaboration with ChatGPT India.

The setup is deceptively simple. A dashcam — or a smartphone mounted on the dashboard — paired with GPS and an accelerometer collects road data during an ordinary drive. The footage is fed to OpenAI's vision models, which detect potholes of different sizes, including distant ones that can resemble speed breakers, and classify them as small, medium, or large. When a pothole is flagged, the app records its exact location and a screenshot, then searches through thousands of government road contracts to match the defect with the project assigned to that stretch.

Each generated report carries a photograph of the pothole, its GPS coordinates, the relevant tender number, and the officer responsible for the road — documented evidence that can be filed with civic authorities. During one test drive to work, Sen's system detected 12 potholes along his route. He built the working prototype in about two days using OpenAI's Codex coding assistant, with Deepanshu Pathak as co-builder, releasing it as open-source software under an MIT license.

"One drive to work got me 12 potholes."

— Gaurav Sen, in the viral demo (via The Better India)

What shipped is more careful than the demo

The viral demo promised instant accountability — a complaint naming the contractor and the responsible officer. The shipped app is narrower and more honest (ToKnow.ai). Pothole Reporter runs in the background on Android while Maps or a call is open, sampling roughly one frame in five, and it also flags garbage and open manholes.

The harder problem is blame. The app scans 3,787 national highway tender rows plus state procurement feeds, but it prints a contractor's name only when official evidence confirms five things at once: the exact road segment, the work scope, the award, the road owner, and the warranty. No record lines up on all five points, so the shipped complaints name no contractor — and the app never submits anything on its own. Instead it drafts an email, a short WhatsApp message, or copyable portal fields carrying the photo, coordinates, and tender reference, then hands the user to the official service.

That restraint is the point. Routing a complaint to the right office can be automated; deciding who is to blame cannot, and the app treats that difference as a hard boundary rather than a marketing line.

A problem measured in lives, not minutes

India's potholes are not a nuisance — they are a public-safety emergency. In 2023 alone, potholes were linked to 5,840 road accidents and 2,161 deaths in India, according to figures cited by The Better India; more than 2,000 Indians die every year in pothole-related accidents.

For Sen, the problem was personal. With his wife pregnant, every trip to the doctor meant driving over potholes; Gizbot reports that his mother-in-law suffered an injury in a road accident. The Bengaluru Development Authority has reportedly shown interest in integrating the system with its own services.

What's next

Coverage now spans all 28 states and 8 union territories, 680 mapped national highway references, and four languages, according to ToKnow.ai. Each user supplies their own OpenAI API key, keeping the project independent at a small cost to the user. The open question is adoption: a four-second complaint is only as good as the civic office that receives it, and whether India's municipal bodies integrate systems like this will determine whether Sen's invention stays a viral demo or becomes infrastructure. For the diaspora, the model travels: NRIs who drive Indian roads on visits home can use the tool directly, and its open-source code is a template for civic accountability anywhere.
